old_entry.title: Donkey Kong
old_entry.subtitle: Donkey Kong Turns a Jump into a Grammar for Video Games
old_entry.summary: On July 9, 1981 Nintendo began the limited Japanese arcade release of Donkey Kong.
body: On July 9, 1981 Nintendo began the limited Japanese arcade release of Donkey Kong. Shigeru Miyamoto built four screens in which a simple story, rescuing Lady from the gorilla, is told through ramps, barrels, elevators and jumps. Jumpman, the future Mario, is born here, bringing a new emphasis on character to the action game. Donkey Kong matters not only because it creates two icons: it shows how animation, readable goals and changing environments can turn an arcade challenge into a small interactive story.

The circuit board of Radar Scope was restructured for Donkey Kong. The Radar Scope hardware, originally inspired by the Namco Galaxian hardware, was designed for a large number of enemies moving around at high speeds, which Donkey Kong does not require, so the development team removed unnecessary functions and reduced the scale of the circuit board. The gameplay and graphics were reworked for updated ROM chips; the existing CPU, sound hardware, and monitor were left intact. The character set, scoreboard, upper HUD display, and font are almost identical to Radar Scope, with palette differences. The Donkey Kong hardware has the memory capacity for displaying 128 foreground sprites at 16x16 pixels each and 256 background tiles at 8x8 pixels each. Mario and all moving objects use single sprites, the taller Pauline uses two sprites, and the larger Donkey Kong uses six sprites.

Each of the four single-screen stages represents 25 meters of the structure Donkey Kong has climbed: 25, 50, 75, and 100 meters. Stage one involves Mario scaling a construction site made of crooked girders and ladders while jumping over or hammering barrels and oil drums tossed by Donkey Kong. Stage two involves climbing a five-story structure of conveyor belts, each of which transport cement pans. The third stage involves the player riding elevators while avoiding bouncing springs. The final stage requires Mario to remove eight rivets from the platforms supporting Donkey Kong; this causes Donkey Kong to fall and the hero to be reunited with Pauline. These four stages combine to form one level.

The game uses graphics and animation for characterization. Donkey Kong smirks upon Mario's demise. Pauline has a pink dress and long hair, and a speech balloon crying "HELP!". Mario, depicted in red overalls and a red cap, is an everyman character, a type common in Japan. Graphical limitations and the low pixel resolution of the small sprites prompted his design. A mustache implies a mouth, a cap obviates the animation of hair, and colored overalls distinguish his arm movements. The artwork of the cabinets and promotional materials make these cartoon-like character designs even more explicit. Pauline, for example, is disheveled like King Kong's Fay Wray in a torn dress and stiletto heels.

original.old_heading: Radar Scope becomes the problem to solve
original.old_body: Donkey Kong also grows from the need to reuse circuits and cabinets left unsold in the United States; Miyamoto recalled that a new program could turn that stock into a different product. The choice needs to be read within the technical and production constraints of its period. Memory, processors, storage, peripherals and pipelines are not neutral background details: they define what can be shown and therefore what can become interaction. A project gains identity when it turns a limitation or capability of the hardware into a recognizable rule. Technology matters here less as a specification list than as a method, making visible the passage from an available tool to a form of play that would previously have been harder to build.

original.old_heading: Jumping changes the relationship with the obstacle
original.old_body: Barrels, girders and height changes ask the player to choose when to stop and when to jump; overcoming danger becomes the central verb that separates the game from many earlier maze-like designs. The mechanic does not live in isolation: it changes the value of space, time and resources, forcing players to build priorities while the situation changes. The result remains readable because the rule produces observable consequences rather than only hidden numbers. That relationship between a local decision and the rhythm of the whole play session is what makes the system memorable. Looking at it today shows how the game turns a simple idea into a grammar learned through attempts, mistakes and anticipation.

original.old_heading: Jumpman, Lady and Kong tell a story before words
original.old_body: The relationship among captor, victim and hero is readable through poses, animation and screen position, allowing an arcade machine to stage recognizable characters without lengthy explanation. Writing does not remain separate from the rules. Goals, characters and transformations gain weight because players encounter them through actions, constraints and consequences, not only during narrative scenes. Story organizes the experience while the system gives the story concrete form. It is a difficult balance: when it works, a plot development also changes how a battle, a space or a choice is read. The work's memory then grows from the connection between what is told and what the player is asked to do.

game.Name: Donkey Kong
game.Overview:
Donkey Kong is a fixed-screen platform game in which the player controls a carpenter originally identified as Jumpman and later known as Mario. Donkey Kong has carried away a woman called Lady, later named Pauline, and taken her to the top of a construction site. Mario must run across platforms, climb ladders, and jump over hazards to reach her before the decreasing bonus counter reaches zero.

The arcade game contains four distinct screen designs, identified as heights of 25, 50, 75, and 100 meters. On the first, Mario climbs a series of sloping girders while Donkey Kong rolls barrels down from above. Some barrels travel down ladders or strike an oil drum at the bottom of the screen, producing fireballs that pursue Mario. Hammers found along the route can temporarily destroy barrels and fireballs, but Mario swings them automatically and cannot jump or climb ladders until their effect expires.

old_entry.title: Oil Panic
old_entry.subtitle: Oil Panic Folds Handheld Play into Two Screens
old_entry.summary: Nintendo released Oil Panic in Japan on May 28, 1982, the first Game & Watch title in the Multi Screen line.
body: Nintendo released Oil Panic in Japan on May 28, 1982, the first Game & Watch title in the Multi Screen line. Its clamshell form divides action between two LCD displays and turns a physical limitation into game structure. On the upper screen the character catches drops of oil; on the lower one he must dump them without hitting people. It is not merely a new container. The movement of attention and action between the two screens shows how hardware form can become level design directly.

The Multi Screen hinge does more than protect the displays when the device is closed. It divides visual space into two planes and forces the player to shift attention quickly between them. Oil Panic uses this separation as part of the challenge: collecting above and dumping below are linked but not simultaneous actions. Hardware imposes a rhythm of attention. Nintendo discovers a relationship that will return decades later with DS: two screens can be more than extra surface; they can organize different functions and timing.

On the upper display, the character must move under falling drops and fill a container. When it is time to empty it, attention shifts to the lower screen, where a mistake can hit people instead of the correct target. The game creates a small working-memory problem: players must remember remaining capacity while anticipating the next movements. LCD segments are fixed and cannot draw free animation, yet combinations of predetermined positions still produce readable, increasing rhythm.

Multi Screen normalizes the idea that a handheld can close, protect its displays and distribute information across two surfaces. Nintendo would return to a similar logic with Nintendo DS, although using far more advanced technology and functions. There is no simple line reducing DS to Oil Panic, but the design continuity matters. Nintendo experimented early with physical form as part of the experience rather than mere packaging. Oil Panic therefore remains a small example of hardware design generating new possibilities for play.

old_entry.title: Final Fantasy III
old_entry.summary: Final Fantasy III is a 1990 role-playing video game developed and published by Square for the Family Computer.
body: Final Fantasy III is a 1990 role-playing video game developed and published by Square for the Family Computer. The third installment in the Final Fantasy series, it follows four orphans from the village of Ur who are chosen by the world's crystals to defeat a great evil and return balance to the world. The gameplay returns to the traditional combat system of the original game, and adds a job system allowing players to switch between character classes with unique abilities.

Development of Final Fantasy III was handled by multiple series veterans including director Hironobu Sakaguchi, designers Hiromichi Tanaka and Kazuhiko Aoki, writer Kenji Terada, composer Nobuo Uematsu, and programmer Nasir Gebelli in his final contribution to the series. Production was a struggle due to data management, and new elements were added to encourage player experimentation. The artwork was a collaborative effort between Koichi Ishii as character and job designer, Yoshitaka Amano as monster designer, and Kazuko Shibuya as main sprite artist. When it completed development, it was described as one of the largest games on the system.

Upon its release in Japan, the game sold 1.4 million copies, and saw generally positive reviews, with most of the praise going to its job system. While ported to multiple platforms in later years, the original was not released outside Japan until 2021. A remake for the WonderSwan Color was planned but ultimately cancelled, while a 3D remake for the Nintendo DS was released internationally in 2006. The game saw the introduction of several recurring elements including a job system, summoned monsters and the Moogle. Terada also adapted it into a manga, and its characters and settings made appearances in later Final Fantasy titles.

editorial_features.title: The people inside the pixels
body: Kazuko Shibuya remembers making the first Final Fantasy's opening landscape under a severe memory limit. A complete new picture would not fit. Hills and sea reused small graphic elements, sometimes flipped to vary their appearance, while the foreground became a black silhouette. The solution kept the travelers readable without supplying every surface with new detail. In her 2013 account, the memorable image grew from choices about what to repeat and what to leave empty, rather than from an unrestricted illustration reduced to screen size.

Shibuya also corrects an appealingly simple account of the game's artwork. Yoshitaka Amano's illustrations did not supply every playable character in a straightforward sequence of adaptations. The internal team created its characters, and some monsters came from Amano's monochrome drawings. Limited available colours required further decisions when those monsters reached the screen; other designers, including Shibuya herself, created monsters too. Her account identifies several kinds of authorship inside one visual style. The person supplying an illustration and the person choosing its pixels were not interchangeable credits.

Koichi Ishii describes another route into the same craft. During the first Final Fantasy, Shibuya was occupied with Rad Racer, so he asked Takashi Tokita to teach him the sprite tools. His first attempt disappeared because he saved it incorrectly. Eventually a working side-view battle display persuaded Hironobu Sakaguchi to use that approach for the characters. Ishii recalls continuing to adjust individual pixels himself. Planning a character, learning a tool and judging an animated result happened together, rather than as neatly separated departments.

For Final Fantasy III, Ishii wanted each job to have its own pose and imagined background. A small palette made those differences difficult. Instead of always reserving one colour for skin, he experimented with bright yellow, khaki and blue to find another family of characters. For the first game, he describes arranging black marks in white mountains for the colour effects produced by a CRT television. The intended picture included the display's behaviour. A sharp modern view can therefore show different relationships from the image these artists were composing.
story_headings: A drawing is not a sprite

editorial_features.title: The people inside the pixels
body: Kazuko Shibuya remembers making the first Final Fantasy's opening landscape under a severe memory limit. A complete new picture would not fit. Hills and sea reused small graphic elements, sometimes flipped to vary their appearance, while the foreground became a black silhouette. The solution kept the travelers readable without supplying every surface with new detail. In her 2013 account, the memorable image grew from choices about what to repeat and what to leave empty, rather than from an unrestricted illustration reduced to screen size.

Shibuya also corrects an appealingly simple account of the game's artwork. Yoshitaka Amano's illustrations did not supply every playable character in a straightforward sequence of adaptations. The internal team created its characters, and some monsters came from Amano's monochrome drawings. Limited available colours required further decisions when those monsters reached the screen; other designers, including Shibuya herself, created monsters too. Her account identifies several kinds of authorship inside one visual style. The person supplying an illustration and the person choosing its pixels were not interchangeable credits.

Koichi Ishii describes another route into the same craft. During the first Final Fantasy, Shibuya was occupied with Rad Racer, so he asked Takashi Tokita to teach him the sprite tools. His first attempt disappeared because he saved it incorrectly. Eventually a working side-view battle display persuaded Hironobu Sakaguchi to use that approach for the characters. Ishii recalls continuing to adjust individual pixels himself. Planning a character, learning a tool and judging an animated result happened together, rather than as neatly separated departments.

For Final Fantasy III, Ishii wanted each job to have its own pose and imagined background. A small palette made those differences difficult. Instead of always reserving one colour for skin, he experimented with bright yellow, khaki and blue to find another family of characters. For the first game, he describes arranging black marks in white mountains for the colour effects produced by a CRT television. The intended picture included the display's behaviour. A sharp modern view can therefore show different relationships from the image these artists were composing.
story_headings: A drawing is not a sprite

old_entry.title: Dragon Quest IV
old_entry.summary: Dragon Quest IV: Chapters of the Chosen, titled Dragon Warrior IV when initially localized to North America, is a 1990 role-playing video game, the fourth installment of the Dragon Quest video game series developed by Chunsoft and published by Enix, and the first of the Zenithian Trilogy.
body: Dragon Quest IV: Chapters of the Chosen, titled Dragon Warrior IV when initially localized to North America, is a 1990 role-playing video game, the fourth installment of the Dragon Quest video game series developed by Chunsoft and published by Enix, and the first of the Zenithian Trilogy. It was originally released for the Famicom on 11 February 1990 in Japan. A North American NES version followed in October 1992, and would be the last Dragon Quest game localized and published by Enix's Enix America Corporation subsidiary prior to its closure in November 1995, as well as the last Dragon Quest game to be localized into English prior to the localization of Dragon Warrior Monsters in December 1999. The game was remade by Heartbeat for the PlayStation, which eventually was available as an Ultimate Hits game. The remake was ported by ArtePiazza to the Nintendo DS, released in Japan November 2007 and worldwide in September 2008. A mobile version based on the Nintendo DS remake was released in 2014 for Android and iOS.

Dragon Quest IV differs from the rest of the series by breaking up the game into five distinct chapters, each of which focuses on a different protagonist or protagonists. The first four are told from the perspective of the Hero's future companions and the fifth one, from the Hero's perspective, brings all the characters together as they start their journey to save the world. The remake adds a sixth chapter.

editorial_features.title: A party acquires a voice
body: Dragon Quest IV's companions could choose their own actions in battle. In a 1989 interview, Yuji Horii and programmer Koichi Nakamura describe the difficulty of making that proposal work. Simply selecting the strongest response did not necessarily make an interesting game. The player needed a meaningful directing role too. Their account preserves uncertainty inside a famous series: a party could suggest independent people through its behaviour, while the same independence risked taking decisions away from the person responsible for getting everyone home alive.

The wagon made that relationship physical. Characters waiting outside a battle could still gain experience while the group travelled across the overworld. Dungeons complicated the arrangement because leaving everyone behind could eventually make those companions too weak to use. Horii and Nakamura describe allowing the wagon into some dungeons to address that problem. A group of characters was therefore also a set of rules about absence. Someone outside the immediate scene still needed a route back into the player's future choices.

In the later Dragon Quest VI interviews, Horii describes writing new town dialogue as events change. Returning to a village after becoming lost could produce another useful conversation instead of exactly the same response. The writing served the player's uncertain route through the world. A line was more than a small piece of exposition placed beside a house. Its availability depended on what had happened, and another version might be needed when the player returned with different knowledge and a different immediate problem.

Programmer Manabu Yamana identifies a less glamorous difficulty: the party might reach an event in many different conditions. A townsperson calling for Hassan would create an awkward scene if Hassan were currently represented by a coffin. The software had to account for such possibilities. Dialogue and party rules could not be finished independently and joined without further work. A convincing conversation depended on checking who was actually present, what state they were in, and whether the words still made sense in that situation.
